title: Effectiveness of a Generate→Validate→Repair Pipeline with Batfish for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (CNSM2026-GenVal-Batfish-PR-v1) to evaluate whether inserting a deterministic Batfish-style validator into a bounded generate→validate→repair pipeline reduces validator-detected deployment-risk configuration errors produced by an LLM intent-to-configuration translator. The preregistered execution contract used shared_initial_generation (one initial model generation per task reused by both baseline and guarded conditions) to isolate repair-triggered differences from generator stochasticity. Under this contract we ran 200 paired tasks (50 per stratum: IOS-like vs JunOS-like × single-step vs multi-step) with declared model gpt-5-mini and a bounded repair budget (≤1 repair attempt per task). All archived scoring artifacts show both arms were validator-clean on every task (baseline = 200/200, guarded = 200/200), yielding paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0, paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap seed archived), and exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. No repairs were invoked (repair count = 0), so the preregistered secondary estimand (repair_success_rate > 50%) is not empirically computable. We reconcile these degenerate outcomes with respect to the preregistered contract, provide a concise summary of the deterministic validator semantics that define the primary outcome, point to the archived execution bundle for reproducibility, and discuss construct/internal/external validity implications and targeted follow-ups supported by the archived artifacts.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-to-configuration translation promises large productivity gains for network operations but raises acute safety concerns: a single incorrect device command can create outages, violate security policies, or introduce routing instability. To reduce deployment risk, recent architectures place deterministic verifiers (sandboxed semantic checkers such as Batfish) in a generate→validate→repair loop, allowing an LLM to propose a candidate configuration, a verifier to flag policy or topology violations, and an automated repair or human gate to correct or block unsafe proposals. Prior studies and position papers recommend verifier-in-the-loop workflows and layered controls, but there is limited controlled, preregistered evidence quantifying the verifier’s marginal benefit when the generator’s sampling variance is suppressed. We therefore asked the confirmatory question preregistered as CNSM2026-GenVal-Batfish-PR-v1: does integrating a deterministic Batfish-like validator into a bounded generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce validator-detected deployment-risk configuration errors compared to LLM-only generation when the initial generation is shared between arms so any observed improvement must come from repair activity? Our contributions are (1) a sealed preregistered paired trial design that isolates repair-mediated gains by using shared_initial_generation, (2) a fully archived execution of 200 paired tasks across four balanced strata with deterministic scoring artifacts, and (3) an artifact-grounded analysis and interpretation of a degenerate null outcome (no validator-detected errors in either arm) with recommendations for follow-up designs.
sections.related_work: LLM-driven NetOps and intent-to-configuration translation have been explored in several recent works that prototype end-to-end pipelines and evaluate safety-controls (e.g., Nguyen Tu et al. 2024; ICNP/NetSoft contributions on intent translation and in-context configuration). Generate→validate→repair and bounded self-correction architectures have been proposed in the LLM-repair literature and adapted to operational workflows (Sang 2025; Okula 2026), while surveys and architectural papers emphasize workflow-centred evaluation, human gates, and sandbox verification (Bilal et al. 2026; Malik 2026). Taxonomies of failure modes for agentic systems underline the need for layered runtime defenses and auditability (Maharaj 2026; Vadlamudi 2026). Our study differs from prior prototype reports by preregistering a single primary estimand in a paired design, fixing the generator’s sample per task (shared_initial_generation) to attribute any difference to repair activity, and archiving deterministic per-episode validator traces and reconciliation artifacts to support reproducible interpretation.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-GenVal-Batfish-PR-v1 and sealed before execution. The single primary estimand is the paired absolute difference in per-task validator-clean rate (guarded − baseline), operationalized as the fraction of tasks for which the final configuration passes the deterministic validator (validator-clean = no validator-detected violations). The preregistration document and the execution manifest in the archived bundle contain the full plan and code used to compute estimands. Design and sampling: We used a paired binary design with 200 distinct intent-to-configuration tasks. Tasks were balanced across four prespecified strata to create controlled heterogeneity: IOS-like single-step (n=50), IOS-like multi-step (n=50), JunOS-like single-step (n=50), and JunOS-like multi-step (n=50). These stratum counts were enforced by the task generator and appear in the authoritative task manifest included in the archive. Shared-initial-generation contract: To isolate repair-mediated effects, a single model generation per task was produced and reused by both the baseline and the guarded evaluation episodes (initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1). This contract intentionally suppresses generator sampling variance so that any discordant pair must arise from repair activity alone. Model, adapter, and repair bound: The declared generator in the execution configuration is gpt-5-mini and the experiment used an adapter family implementing a bounded generate→validate→repair transformation with at most one repair attempt per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Validator semantics: The harm-oracle is a deterministic Batfish-style verifier used as the primary validator. In both preregistration and execution the validator evaluated candidate configurations against an explicit set of operational invariants: (a) reachability constraints (expected intra-VLAN and inter-VLAN paths), (b) ACL/policy compliance (no new permit/deny contradictions vs intent constraints), (c) routing inconsistencies and routing-loop/path anomalies, (d) interface-state and workflow invariants (e.g., make-before-break constraints and required shutdown/configure/restore sequences), and (e) forbidden or dangerous commands as flagged by a command-safety detector. An episode is labelled validator-detected-error if any of these checks reports a failing condition; validator traces record validation_before and validation_after states, violation_count, and encoded violation entries. Analysis plan and inference: The primary confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes (α=0.05). We estimate absolute risk reduction with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed archived). The preregistered power calculation targeted a detectable absolute difference of 10 percentage points with n≈200 paired tasks under McNemar discordant-pair assumptions. Missingness and sensitivity: A complete-pair policy was preregistered (exclude pairs with technical failures); a sensitivity analysis was defined that treats failed guarded episodes conservatively as errors if necessary. Reproducible artifacts: The full experiment harness, raw responses, per-episode validator traces, task manifest and scoring records are archived in the execution bundle; reviewers can inspect the authoritative task manifest and execution manifest to reproduce selection, strata assignment, and scoring.
sections.results: Execution and accounting: The run completed the preregistered 400 episodes (200 tasks × 2 conditions) with zero failed episodes. Provider accounting matched the shared-initial contract: the run used 200 model calls (one per task) and the same initial candidate was reused for both conditions per task. Deterministic reconciliation and analysis logs confirm episode accounting consistency and absence of technical exclusions. Primary outcome: Aggregated scoring artifacts show baseline validator-clean = 200/200 and guarded validator-clean = 200/200. The four-cell paired contingency table contains n_11 = 200 (both-clean), n_10 = 0 (guarded-only-clean), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-clean), and n_00 = 0 (both-error). The point estimate for the paired difference (guarded − baseline) is 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; the paired-bootstrap (10,000 resamples) 95% percentile CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.0], reflecting the degenerate data. Repair activity and secondary estimand: Because no validator-detected errors occurred for any initial candidate, the bounded repair policy was never invoked (repair_count = 0) and the preregistered secondary estimand (repair_success_rate) is not empirically computable from these data. Representative artifact examples: Per-episode canonicalized scoring records and validator traces (including validation_before/validation_after and normalized_configuration fields) are archived and include representative episodes across difficulty patterns. Diagnostic artifacts and logs in the archive show that contamination checks flagged no items and that validator violation_count was zero in all scoring records. Statistical interpretation: The degenerate contingency table implies no observable marginal benefit for the guarded adapter under the executed contract and task bank; this is a concrete, reproducible null rather than an inconclusive non-significant trend. The confidence interval collapse to a single point (0.0) is a direct consequence of the lack of discordant pairs.
sections.discussion: Two artifact-grounded readings of the result are supported by the archived evidence. First, for every preregistered task the single shared initial candidate generated by gpt-5-mini satisfied the deterministic validator’s checks; validator traces record violation_count = 0 consistently. Second, because no validator-detected errors occurred, the bounded repair loop could not execute and therefore could not produce corrections; the experiment therefore cannot offer evidence on the repair loop’s effectiveness under this contract. Design trade-offs and sensitivity: The shared_initial_generation contract increases causal clarity about repair-mediated effects by eliminating generator sampling variance; however, this choice reduces sensitivity to generator-sampling-induced failures and therefore lowers the chance of observing discordant pairs that would give the repair loop an opportunity to act. An independent-generation design (distinct generator calls per condition) would increase the empirical probability that baseline produces failing candidates relative to guarded, raising sensitivity to repair effectiveness but conflating generation variance with repair efficacy. Validator fidelity and external realism: The deterministic Batfish-style validator enforces a curated set of invariants; in production, device-specific quirks, vendor feature gaps, or additional operational checks may reveal errors not captured by our sandbox. Thus, whether a verifier materially improves field outcomes depends jointly on (1) generator sampling dispersion (how often the model proposes unsafe candidates in realistic use), (2) validator fidelity to device semantics, and (3) repair policy richness (single bounded repair vs iterative synthesis and programmatic repairs). Follow-up experiments enabled by the archive: the preserved task manifest and response traces allow reproducible follow-ups that change one axis at a time—examples include switching to independent condition generation, increasing repair budget and enabling iterative repair strategies, extending the validator harm-oracle to simulate vendor quirks, or injecting adversarial prompt perturbations to stress robustness. Operational implications: Practitioners should view verifier-in-the-loop architectures as one of several levers: they are most likely to show measurable operational benefit when generator sampling variance yields a non-trivial rate of unsafe initial candidates or when the validator captures harm signals that would occur on target devices. For environments where a generator already produces correct, policy-compliant candidates with high probability, a bounded verifier may be redundant for some classes of tasks.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired trial to measure the marginal effect of a deterministic Batfish-style validator in a bounded generate→validate→repair pipeline under a shared_initial_generation contract. For the synthetic 200-task bank and declared generator (gpt-5-mini) used here, every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator; both baseline and guarded arms were validator-clean on all tasks, producing an exact paired difference of 0.0 (95% CI [0.0,0.0]; McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were invoked, so repair efficacy was not observed. These artifact-grounded results do not refute the potential value of verifier-assisted workflows; instead, they show that preregistered contract choices (shared vs independent generation), task-bank challenge level, validator expressiveness, and repair policy jointly determine whether verifier assistance yields an observable benefit. The archived execution bundle contains the task manifest, raw responses, per-episode validator traces, paired contingency tables, and reconciliation logs necessary to reproduce the run and to design targeted follow-ups that vary generation independence, repair budget, model families, validator semantics, or adversarial conditions. We encourage follow-up preregistered comparisons that use the archived artifacts as a baseline and that explicitly trade off generator variance and repair opportunity to quantify repair-mediated gains in realistic settings.

limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to a synthetic public task corpus and a deterministic Batfish-style sandbox; results do not generalize to production devices, multi-vendor heterogeneity, or richer harm oracles.
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini) and a single bounded repair budget (≤1 repair); no cross-model or multi-iteration repair claims are made.

The preregistered shared_initial_generation contract produced exactly one shared initial generation per task that was reused for both conditions; this reduces sensitivity to generator stochasticity and therefore reduces the likelihood of observing discordant pairs arising purely from generation variance.

The repair loop was never invoked because baseline produced zero validator-detected errors; therefore the preregistered secondary hypothesis about repair-success (>50%) could not be empirically evaluated.

Contamination and template-alignment risk: automated contamination checks recorded no flagged items, but pretraining memorization or template-alignment remains a construct-validity threat that automated checks cannot fully eliminate.
Adversarial and prompt-injection scenarios were not included; the study does not assess robustness under targeted attacks.
